title: both either neither
subtitle: both of them / neither of us
summary: Use both, either and neither to talk about two people or things, with both + plural and either/neither + singular.

lesson.heading: Two people or things
lesson.text: We use **both**, **either** and **neither** when we talk about *two* things or people. **both** = the two; **either** = one or the other; **neither** = not one and not the other.

examples.text: Rebecca has two children. **Both** are married. (**both** = the two children)
Would you like tea or coffee? You can have **either**. (**either** = tea or coffee)
*A:* Do you want to go to the cinema or the theatre? *B:* **Neither**. I want to stay at home.

lesson.heading: either and neither

left.label: either
examples: '**Either**. I don't mind.' (= tea or coffee)

right.label: neither
right.text: **neither** = not + either, so the verb is positive.
examples: *A:* Do you go to work by car or by bus? *B:* **Neither**. I always walk.

lesson.note: Say *I don't want either*, not ~~I don't want neither~~.

lesson.heading: both of / either of / neither of
lesson.text: Before **the**, **these**, **those**, **my**, **your** or a name we use **of**. With **both** the word **of** is not necessary, but with **either** and **neither** it is.

examples.text: I haven't read **either of these books**.
I like **both of those pictures**. *or* I like **both those pictures**.

lesson.heading: both of them / neither of us
lesson.text: Before **them**, **us** and **you** we always use **of**: **both of them**, **either of us**, **neither of you**.

examples.text: Paul has got two sisters. **Both of them** are married.
Sue and I didn't eat anything. **Neither of us** was hungry.
Who are those two people? I **don't** know **either of them**.

lesson.text: **both** takes a plural verb (*Both cups **are** empty*), but **neither** takes a singular verb (*Neither answer **is** right*).

exercises.prompt: Last year I went to Paris and Rome. I liked ___ cities very much.
It was a good football match. ___ teams played well.
exercises.explanation: The two teams played well, so both teams.

exercises.prompt: It wasn't a good football match. ___ team played well.
exercises.explanation: Not one team and not the other, so neither team (singular noun).

exercises.prompt: 'Is your friend English or American?' '___ . She's Australian.'
exercises.explanation: She is not English and not American, so Neither.

exercises.prompt: There were two pictures on the wall. I didn't like ___ them.
exercises.explanation: After a negative verb we use either of them.

exercises.prompt: Which nouns go after both, and which go after either or neither?
I invited Donna and Mike to the party, but ___ them came.
exercises.explanation: Donna didn't come and Mike didn't come, so neither of them came.

exercises.prompt: 'Do you work or are you a student?' '___ . I work and I'm a student too.'
exercises.explanation: The answer is yes to the two things, so Both.

exercises.prompt: Paula and I didn't know the time because ___ us had a watch.
exercises.explanation: Before us we always use of: neither of us.

exercises.prompt: There are two buses at the stop. One goes to the airport and the other goes to the airport too. ___ go to the airport.
exercises.explanation: both + plural noun + plural verb: Both buses go ...
Neither of Paul's sisters is married. Before a name we need of.

exercises.prompt: A man and a woman both said 'No' to 'Are you interested in sport?'. Put the words in order.
exercises.answer: Neither of them is interested in sport.
exercises.explanation: neither of them + singular verb is.
